plan.concept: RANSAC (Random Sample Consensus) iteratively estimates model parameters from noisy data containing outliers by testing minimal random subsets of points.
learningObjectives: After engaging with this figure, the student will understand how RANSAC uses a minimal sample set (2 points for a line) to generate a model hypothesis
The student will be able to explain how the inlier threshold determines which data points support a given hypothesis
The student will understand why repeating this randomized process with different samples eventually finds the correct global consensus model despite abundant outliers
plan.keyInsight: Instead of fitting a model to all points (which fails due to outliers), RANSAC finds the 'truth' by finding the model that gets the most votes (inliers) from small random guesses.

interactions.label: RANSAC Iteration
interactions.effect: Changes the selected pairs of points (highlighted in red), the fitted line, and the resulting inliers (colored blue).
interactions.teaches: How random selection of points generates different candidate lines, some of which are poor fits while others capture the true data trend.

interactions.label: Inlier Threshold
interactions.effect: Visualizes the width of the tolerance band around the line, changing which points fall close enough to be colored as blue inliers.
interactions.teaches: The trade-off of the tolerance parameter: too small misses true points; too large includes obvious noise/outliers.

demo_steps.title: Hypothesis Generation
demo_steps.narration: Look at the two solid red points. RANSAC begins by randomly selecting the absolute minimum number of points needed to define a model—in this case, 2 points to define a line. A candidate line (the red line) is drawn directly through them.
demo_steps.focus: The two red sample points and the red line spanning between them.

demo_steps.title: Evaluating consensus
demo_steps.narration: Notice the single light blue point close to the line. With our current tolerance threshold, only this point falls close enough to be considered an 'inlier'. This gives us a total consensus of only 3 inliers (the 2 sample points + 1 neighbor), meaning this candidate line is likely a poor fit.
demo_steps.focus: The blue inlier point and the text label '3 inliers' near the line.

demo_steps.title: Finding the True Consensus
demo_steps.narration: Now move the iteration slider to try a different random sample. Notice how sampling two points that actually align with the main cluster of data generates a new line that gains a much higher consensus (more blue inliers), revealing the true underlying structure of the data.
demo_steps.focus: The new set of red sample points aligning with the main curve/line of data, causing many points to turn blue.

demo_steps.title: The Role of Tolerance
demo_steps.narration: Adjust the Inlier Threshold slider. If the threshold is set too low, even valid points are rejected as outliers; if set too high, unrelated random noise gets falsely counted as part of the consensus. Tuning this threshold is crucial for RANSAC to successfully distinguish signal from noise.
demo_steps.focus: The widening tolerance region around the line and the rapid change in the number of blue-colored inliers.

plan.reconstructionNotes: A 2D scatter plot with a black vertical Y-axis and a black horizontal X-axis. Points are plotted as circles. The baseline data should feature a visible upward-sloping linear trend of points (the 'true' model) alongside several scattered outlier points. In iteration 1, two points that do not match the main trend are highlighted in solid red, with a red line passing through them. Points within a small distance threshold of this red line are colored solid light blue (inliers), while other points remain empty white circles with black outlines. A text annotation displays the count of inliers (e.g., '3 inliers'). Changing the iteration slider repositions the red line to match other randomly sampled point pairs.
